speechtext: FAILURE TO SETTLE LONGSHOREMEN DISPUTE ___LEGISLATION TO APPOINT PUBLIC ADMINISTRATOR-POSSIBLE MORNING SITTING

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members know, my deputy minister, or rather my assistant deputy minister and I went to Vancouver on Friday last with a view to trying to bring about the resumption of work in the docks on our west coast. Several approaches to a settlement were tested during the past few days but I regret to report that my efforts were unsuccessful.
I reported to the Prime Minister on my return, and it has been decided that in the national interest legislation must be submitted to parliament forthwith-legislation which will include the appointment of a public administrator so that operations on the waterfront may be resumed in the shortest possible time.
As one might expect, when this regrettable situation developed instructions were given for the preparation of draft legislation. I have been working on this legislation all morning and will be working on it again this afternoon, because in view of the different factors involved I can assure the house this is an extremely complicated matter. It is not like the British Columbia coast steamship case; it is not like the maritime trusteeship. There are a number of special factors to be considered, including the extent of the coverage and the number of institutions which might be affected.
I have suggested to the leader of the house that arrangements might be made for a special sitting of the house, possibly tomorrow morning. The improvements in the original draft legislation may well take several hours. Since I shall be making a statement when the bill is presented to the house, I would prefer not to make any further statement at this time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
At long last the government
has decided to act. I do not know of any previous occasion when the economy has been allowed to suffer to such a degree as in this case, certainly not in the last few years. There was a total disregard by the government of the need for action.
Today, finally, after days and days of uncertainty-
Negotiations.

-the government has decided to do that which it should have done earlier. As to the suggestion of the appointment of a public administrator, I put that before the house yesterday. For the past ten days, day after day, the people of Canada have witnessed a government uncertain in its course. However, now that they have finally decided to act, we can at least say that this matter will receive the attention by parliament which it should have received days and days ago.

We
all regret that the minister has not been successful in bringing both parties together in the dispute which has tied up the British Columbia ports for the past ten days.
We in this party have been pointing out for some time that this situation constitutes a national emergency, with grain cars backing up to the prairies, with perishable goods not being unloaded, and with men being laid off in other industries because of the lack of shipping facilities. I think it is unnecessary to make any comment on the legislation the government intends to bring down, until we see the bill.
I hope the government will keep in mind the fact that the compromise proposal which the minister drafted while he was in Vancouver was accepted by the workers and that the stevedoring companies refused to accept that compromise. Therefore in any legislation to set up a public administrator it seems to me totally unnecessary to place the union under a public administrator. It is the companies in this case which are refusing to end their lockout. They are the ones that

December 7, 1966
Labour Relations
need to be brought under a public administrator, in order that the ports can be operated. We are anxious to have the ports operating as quickly as possible and we will do everything in our power to facilitate the consideration of this legislation. We hope the government will bring it down just as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, since this strike is quite similar to the railway strike with which the government has been faced recently, I think the minister is making a very wise decision for the time being when he says he will introduce a bill designed to appoint a public trustee in order to get both parties concerned to enter into an agreement.
Some will say, as just did the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), that the government is acting too late, but I believe the minister has given both parties concerned, employers and workers, enough time to discuss freely and he intervened in an attempt to submit proposals to either group. In my opinion, it was necessary for the government to allow time to both parties lest it be accused of restricting the rights of management and labour.
In my opinion, since all other means have been exhausted, I trust that the bill will finally enable the cause of the majority to prevail; indeed, parliament must see to it that the common good takes precedence over private interests. Therefore, I think that our discussions should be directed to that end, since it is our duty to protect not only a group of citizens, but the entire community. I hope that this bill will help to bring out that principle.

Mr. Speaker, a few days ago we had an opportunity to debate this particular problem to some extent on an adjournment motion moved by my colleague from Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Johnston). During the course of that discussion I said that we sympathized with the minister in his desire to give all possible opportunity for the dispute to be settled without government interference or participation. But now the time has come when some definite action must be taken.
We appreciate the measure that is to be introduced, because we believe it is very urgent that shipping get under way immediately. The results of a continued stoppage 
at this time will be catastrophic so far as the Pacific coast and the entire western part of Canada are concerned, and therefore action must be taken immediately. However, Mr. Speaker, reference has been made to the compromise proposal that was offered by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson). I can understand the reluctance with which that was greeted, because there are certain very fundamental principles involved. For instance, there is the matter of the position of the foremen in the labour-management picture, and also the relationship between the minister's proposal and decisions by the Labour Relations Board. All these things have an important bearing on the matter, and must be gone into thoroughly before we can pass judgment on the legislation. However, once again may I say I believe it is absolutely imperative that shipping get under way, and that we would welcome legislation in order to achieve that objective.

speechtext:

8.	Has it any regular channels or communication with the Consumers' Association of Canada and, if so, what are they?

10.	Have studies been made to discover what specific fields of consumer education should be stressed?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: CONSUMER SECTION OF DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
1.	The Consumer Section was formally established in 1939 but home economist service was provided earlier through divisional staff.
2.	Authorized establishment includes: 11 home economists, three technicians, five clerical staff, one part-time kitchen assistant.
3.	Expenditure for 1965-66 was $107,366. Budget for 1966-67 is $178,000.
4.	The functions of the section are to provide a national service to consumers on the buying and use of Canadian food products of agricultural origin, to increase the consumption of such foods, to broaden consumer understanding and appreciation of grading and marketing regulations administered by the department, and to collaborate with commodity divisions of the department in the development and evaluation of grade standards for agricultural products.
5.	The section conducts consumer research alone and in conjunction with other divisions of the department.
6.	Techniques vary with the project. Taste panels are utilized to keep abreast of consumer preferences. Supply and demand studies of the Economics Branch are used for short term consumer price outlooks. Trends in consumption patterns are studied as a guide to determine current and future consumer requirements.
7.	Information is conveyed to the consumer by publications, exhibits, press releases, radio tapes and scripts, television films, and speaking engagements. Consumers communicate with the section by letter, telephone and in person at exhibits and meetings at which staff speak to groups.
8.	There is constant communication with the Consumers' Association of Canada by letter, telephone, staff membership in the organization, and personal contact.
9.	No formal studies have been conducted by the section but certain commodity legislation administered by the department sets

out container size limitations. These limitations were developed based on consumer preferences for container sizes then on the market.
10.	The specific fields stressed are those related to the section's functions and no formal studies have been made to determine which of these should be stressed at any particular time. Commodity consumption promotion is accented in relation to supply and price.

Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) recently issued a press release to the effect that, again this year, ice-breakers on the St. Lawrence will not be commissioned to clear the seaway for shipping, but will simply prevent ice-jams and floods occurring in the spring.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, to show that this is a definite matter of urgent public importance, let me remind the house that last year 120 ocean-going ships reached Montreal and that 200 are expected to this year. However, if the St. Lawrence river is not cleared, it will hamper and interfere with winter shipping. It is urgent that the matter be discussed without delay and that decisions be taken as soon as possible, so that shipping companies, knowing that the St. Lawrence river will not be open to shipping again this year, will not plan to use that great seaway. If we now have a fruitful discussion on the problem and if the Minister of Transport is in a position to announce that ice-breakers on the St. Lawrence will clear the way for ships to reach the port of Montreal, shipping on the St. Lawrence will increase as well as port operations at Montreal, for the benefit of the whole country.
A debate is most urgent, Mr. Speaker, as is evidenced by the fact that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) intends to ask leave to have a special sitting of the house tomorrow morning to deal with the matter of the west coast tie-up due to a strike.
The port of Montreal and those along the St. Lawrence are closed because of ice conditions and the Minister of Transport can easily put at the disposal of the authorities of those ports the icebreakers required to ensure year round navigation on the river.

Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the cases are similar: on the one hand the ports are closed because of a strike, on the other, because of ice conditions. It is possible to solve both problems provided we can discuss them and arrive at a decision.
That is why I believe the matter is pressing, for winter will soon set in.
You are undoubtedly aware, Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as your home is close to the St. Lawrence seaway, that according to the latest news the St. Lawrence seaway will be closed tomorrow morning for fear of a freeze-up in the next few days. Under those circumstances, I feel the matter is urgent. If we wait another week, our winter navigation may be a failure, and the shipping companies in Europe, South America and Africa, which might otherwise be interested in shipping by way of the St. Lawrence, may not do so because of the recent statement of the Department of Transport. For that reason, I would ask you to allow debate on this urgent and important matter of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
Before going any further, Mr. Speaker, I wish to pay tribute to all the men and women in the forces for the enormous effort they have put forward during the past two years. That they have been able to keep the defence forces of this country at a high state of readiness, contribute to our several international commitments and, at the same time, manage this fundamental reorganization of the forces is truly a magnificent achievement. The associate minister and myself wish to express our deep appreciation to the Canadian servicemen and women for all they have done and for the vigour with which these tasks have been undertaken.
The white paper on defence tabled in 1964 dealt at some length with defence policy. It reviewed Canadian defence policy since 1945 and the principal considerations affecting future policy as they were seen at the time the paper was presented. While there have been some rather important developments in the last two years affecting NATO and other areas of the world, the basic conclusions contained in the white paper continue to be valid today.
I do not propose, therefore, to go over this area in detail again at this time.
National Defence Act Amendment
It continues to be our view that Canada's participation in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization is a worth-while contribution to world stability; that our NORAD undertakings are of value and are not likely to require major modifications in the immediate future unless a decision is made by the United States to deploy an antimissile defence; that the contributions Canada is able to make to the United Nations peacekeeping operations have provided and will continue to provide Canada with opportunities to contribute to the control of potentially dangerous situations outside the NATO area.
Forces for the direct protection of Canada remain necessary. While direct attack on Canadian territory is very low in the scale of probability, it is essential to provide appropriate surveillance of our territory and its sea approaches as well as to have the capability of dealing with lodgments of enemy forces in the unlikely event they should occur.
In the course of my remarks I will be saying something about the forces we have available for all of these purposes and the progress that has been made toward the objectives set out in the white paper.
The Canadian armed services, at the end of the second world war, were three distinct entities, each of which was largely independent of the others in the management of its military affairs. In the next several years a number of external and internal influences combined to foster increasing interdependence and co-operation. This process, in the circumstances of the post-war period, led logically to the integration of the three services, as announced by the government in the white paper on defence in March, 1964. A brief review of some of the main factors affecting the management of Canada's defence in the two postwar decades will illustrate my point.
One of the first significant events was the appointment of a single Minister of National Defence. During the second world war, in Canada there were separate political heads for each of the main branches of the armed forces. The reorganization of the government defence machinery after the war led to the appointment in 1946 of a single minister responsible for defence, with the provision subsequently in 1950 for the appointment of
10818	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment associate ministers as appropriate. The appointment of a single political head for the Department of National Defence was bound to encourage a more unified approach to defence problems.
The establishment of a single scientific organization to serve the military arms of the department was consistent with the trend. The outstanding contribution of scientific research to the war potential of the world war II allies made it evident that defence research was an essential element of any future military activity. In view of this, the Defence Research Board was established on April 1, 1947, to conduct and sponsor research on a wide variety of military problems and to provide scientific advice to the Canadian forces. It is significant that this agency provided for centralized direction of laboratories formerly components of the individual services and for the management of research activity covering the whole spectrum of defence science including the specialized problems of the maritme land and air environments.
Not long afterwards important legislation affecting defence was passed by parliament. The legal basis for Canadian defence activities of all kinds was overhauled and modernized in the National Defence Act passed in 1950, which is chapter 184 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952. This act applied the same rules of Canadian military law and justice to members of all three services and introduced a common approach to all other legal aspects of defence. Also, the Queen's Regulations and Orders, although issued separately for the three services, established standard regulations in many areas affecting all of the services.
Another contributing factor was a change in the method of appointing the chairman of the chiefs of staff committee. The chiefs of staff committee, originally created in 1927 as the joint staff committee, was reconstituted and renamed in January 1939 after the appointment of a chief of the air staff was created. The chairmanship was decided by seniority among the service chiefs of staff until early in 1951 when legislation was passed providing for the appointment of a full-time chairman

DEBATES	December 7, 1966
independent of the services. His terms of reference specifically required him to "co-ordinate the training and operations of the Canadian forces". Although not vested with executive authority over the services, the chairman of the chiefs of staff committee was an important influence in the adoption of common standards in many areas of defence.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Despite its inadequacies, the committee system in the defence department did have a unifying influence which deserves mention. The defence council has been the senior committee of the department. Prior to the reorganization of Canadian forces headquarters, its active members included the minister, the associate minister, the chairman of the chiefs of staff committee, the chiefs of staff, the chairman of the Defence Research Board and the deputy minister. It was, therefore, a natural forum for the resolution of inter-service differences although, in practice, much of its attention was devoted to minor administrative matters.
The chiefs of staff committee usually met more frequently than the defence council and was more intimately concerned with immediate and pressing problems, particularly those involving military policy and operations. Subsidiary to these two committees were the personnel members committee formed in 1944 and the principal supply officers committee formed in 1947. Many other inter-service committees dealt with specific or technical aspects of personnel and supply problems and military planning and operations involving more than one service.
Prior to Bill No. C-90-1964-there was really no alternative to the use of committees. They were needed to reconcile the different policies and practices of the services. It is recognized that a committee structure does not usually provide a decisive or effective mechanism for executive action. Progress was made, nevertheless, in co-ordinating and standardizing the policies and procedures of the services.
Since the end of the second world war a number of steps were also taken to consolidate some of the specialized activities of the services. An example of this was the tri-service approach in the Canadian services colleges. It was decided that all officer cadets at
December 7, 1966	COMMONS
services colleges would complete the last two years of their course at the Royal Military College. The service affiliation of the cadets did not change but they were brought together and exposed to the identical academic atmosphere during a critical period in their education. Another example was the integration of the legal services at the end of the second world war. Then during the 1950's the medical and chaplain services were both integrated.
It was clear that the tendency was in the direction of integration, particularly in fields where it was essential to conserve scarce professional and technical resources.
The complexity and rising cost of managing logistics problems were influential in forcing more co-ordination in the area of military supply. It was recognized in both Canada and the United States immediately after the war that changes in materiel identification and control were essential. Cataloguing and identification procedures had developed in a haphazard fashion under wartime pressures and major changes were essential. The pioneering effort of the United States in this field was ultimately adopted by NATO and embodied in two standardization agreements. These were formally accepted by Canada and intensive work has been carried on by the services to achieve standard catalogue references for all materiel in the military supply systems. The concept of common cataloguing was approved by the principal supply officers committee in November, 1961, and was applied to a limited range of equipment. This foreshadowed the general application of the concept in 1964. In addition, other functions have been managed by a single service. As examples, dental, food procurement and military postal services were provided by the army for all three services.
Underlying the major revision of Canada's defence policy announced in 1964 is the concept that any organization, military or civilian, which does not adapt to a changing environment will surely decline. In the early 1960's it became apparent that two aspects of this problem demanded special attention. They were the management and control structure, and the influence of rising costs.
National Defence Act Amendment
One of the issues stressed in a statement before the special committee on defence in 1964 was the number of senior officials with direct access to the minister. I pointed out at that time:
With the present prerogative of the chiefs of staff to come directly to the minister with their problems and submissions, there are many cases where proposals are dealt with by the minister in isolation . . , This will be overcome in our proposed organization by the fact that all military proposals will come through one channel, and, therefore, must in effect be co-ordinated before they come to the attention of the minister.
The desirability of adopting sound management principles and a simplified chain of command was reiterated in a subsequent statement I made before the same committee.
X think it-the Canadian defence organization-will be the best military organization, the most responsive to co-ordinated action, and that because of its simplified lines of communication it will be able to develop new concepts and techniques more quickly and more rapidly than it would have had it not been reorganized.

speechtext:
This point of view reflected the growing complexity of defence choices which often involved political, economic and scientific problems as well as issues of military effectiveness.
As part of the reorganization plan, it was announced in 1964 that the Department of National Defence would be introducing modern new management tools applicable to defence problems. Members may recall the section in the report of the royal commission on government organization which stated:
Not only is the relative size of the "administrative tail" growing steadily in all military forces- for budgeting, accounting, supply, construction and general administration; in addition, among the operational elements themselves there is a rapid increase in the technical content of the work, a large element being common to all three services. Consequently, there is a growing range of activities of common concern to the services, for which the traditional basis of organization is unsuited. It is increasingly recognized that to maintain three separate organizations for such functions is uneconomic. Moreover, the chronic scarcity of many of the skills involved cannot be ignored.
This problem was recognized and a number of new management systems are being introduced.
A system of defence programming has been established. It provides for programming for
10820	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment defence through a logical sequence of steps from the establishment of defence policies and objectives to the final output of defence forces to meet those objectives. The process is designed to produce data and options which assist in taking decisions that are calculated to achieve the objectives in the most economical way. It also establishes, once decisions are taken, the basis for systematic follow-through until the program is completed. The long-term programming is the basis for annual budgeting and ensures that the two are consistent. This system is now functioning but it will not be perfected for some time as it requires the accumulation of basic costing data, the development of analytic methods and the training of staff in the various techniques required.
Other innovations to assist in management are being introduced. These include the installation of responsibility accounting and program budgeting. A model has been constructed and is being tested in air transport command and later the approved system will be applied to other commands. A third program is redesigning the present supply systems into a single one incorporating modern techniques in this field. The work of installing a single automated pay system is also well advanced.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
These advances rely heavily on the application of modern methods of data processing which can be introduced more realistically and productively in an integrated force. Perhaps of more importance they place great demands on men highly trained in modern management techniques who are in short supply. Integration permitted these very valuable manpower resources to be used much more effectively because in many cases identical problems no longer have to be dealt with for each service separately.
The impact of sharply rising costs for personnel, maintenance and operations had been observed for some time and its consequences for Canada's defence activities were strongly emphasized in the policy discussions of 1964. It was recognized that the total funds available for defence were not likely to change greatly so that money available for capital equipment would inevitably decline drastically unless something was done about it.
In the white paper on defence (1964) and previously in the report of the Royal Commission on Government Organization, great

DEBATES	December 7, 1966
stress was placed on the importance of reducing manpower costs associated with headquarters, training and similar establishments, as well as operating and maintenance expenses which could be cut without impairing operational efficiency. The elimination of duplication and triplication of staff and facilities was one of the main justifications for the integration of the services. This was particularly true in the support and administration functions.
I wish to put this in more concrete terms by comparing expenditures in the fiscal year 1962-63 with estimates for the fiscal year 1966-67, both years being close to the same level of approximately $1,575 million. The conclusion is sometimes reached because the figures are approximately the same that there have been no reductions in costs in the defence department. If I apply to the actual strengths of military and civilian personnel employed in the department in 1962-63 the pay, allowance and salary rates applicable in 1966-67, the costs for those personnel would now be $1,141 million. Adding to this the costs of approximately $335 million applicable in both years for other upkeep costs such as the maintenance of aircraft, vehicles, buildings, etc., I have a total figure of $1,476 million. If this had been allowed to happen, provision for all of the capital costs including military equipment, construction and development would have had to be reduced to $97 million in 1966-67; compare this to the $327 million available in the budget. In other words, a reduction in the capital program of about 70 per cent from that provided in the 1966-67 estimates would have been necessary.
The facts are clear and incontrovertible. Either the defence budget had to be substantially increased or substantial cost reductions had to be made. Otherwise, funds would simply not be available for the capital expenditures that are essential to effective military forces. These pressures will continue. The integration through unification process will generate important new cost reductions for some years to come. It should not be expected that these will match the increasing costs in current dollars from year to year, but without them we would face much higher defence budgets to maintain defence forces at approximately the level we have today.

speechtext:
Let me continue my statement.
After considering the factors of management and control, the influence of rising costs, personnel considerations, the nature of modern warfare and the influence of technology, it was necessary to apply general conclusions reached to the specific military requirements of Canada. If we were to maintain useful forces to meet our national and international commitments we had two choices. We must greatly increase defence spending or reorganize our forces. The decision was to reorganize.
As you can see then, the decision to embark on the integration program leading to unification of the forces was made only after a most careful and thorough study of all relevant factors. Once the policy decision was taken, the next step was the appointment by the chiefs of staff of a planning group of senior officers and departmental officials to determine the structure of Canadian forces headquarters. Their planning was carried out concurrently with the consideration by parliament of the amendments to the National Defence Act required to authorize the reorganization.
The third step was the passage of Bill C-90 which provided for the substitution of a single chief of defence staff for the individual service chiefs of staff. This bill was given royal assent on July 16, 1964 and on August 1, 1964 the chief of the defence staff and the heads of the new functional branches at Canadian forces headquarters were appointed.
On the basis of the experience of the first year, some changes were made. Thus, two years after the constitution of the functional branches at headquarters the four branch heads are: the vice-chief of the defence staff, the chief of personnel, the chief of technical services, and the comptroller general. I propose to comment briefly on the responsibilities of the chief of the defence staff and each of the branch chiefs and to discuss briefly the responsibilities of the deputy minister, the Defence Research Board and the defence council.
The appointment of a single chief of the defence staff on August 1, 1964 was the keystone of the reorganized command structure.
National Defence Act Amendment It provided that one man would be responsible to the minister for the control and administration of the Canadian forces. The new position combined the functions of the chairman of the chiefs of staff committee and the chiefs of staff of the three services. It meant that the three services were no longer independent entities for the purpose of control and administration. Thus military command and management came into line with the unified policy direction which was established with the appointment of a single minister responsible for defence in 1946.
The vice-chief of the defence staff is primarily responsible for military operations. He has three deputies. The deputy chief plans is concerned with intelligence and strategic planning. The deputy chief operations has under his direction three directors general who supervise maritime, land and air operations and determine operational requirements. The deputy chief reserves administers the reserve forces and cadet organizations, and is responsible for the planning of the military aspects of survival activities and emergency assistance to the civil authorities. This he does through regional offices across Canada. Reporting also to the vice-chief are the director general operational research and the director general programs. The establishment of the operational research function under the vicechief of the defence staff consolidates the activities of groups previously attached to the three services and to the Defence Research Board. The director general programs is responsible for compiling and maintaining the defence programming system I mentioned earlier.
The chief of personnel and the deputy chief of personnel formulate and administer personnel policy affecting individuals of all ranks from the time they enter the service until their retirement. Directly concerned with this function are the following five directors general: director general senior appointments, director general administration, director general postings and careers, director general training and recruiting, and director general personnel plans and requirements. The offices of the surgeon general, the director general dental services and the chaplains general also constitute a part of the chief of personnel branch. In addition, the director general centennial, who is responsible for military participation

The chief of technical services is responsible for a large and complex area of military activity. He is in charge of all engineering and development activity related to capital equipment programs, plans and policies for the procurement, storage, distribution, inspection, maintenance and disposal of materiel; and for the design, provision and maintenance of accommodation and other military facilities. Under his direction there are three deputy chiefs: deputy chief engineering, deputy chief logistics and deputy chief construction engineering. There is also a scientific deputy.

The comptroller general and deputy comptroller general are responsible for the administration of financial and general management services. Specifically, this embraces the development of the organizational structure of the Canadian forces, the allocation of authorized manpower resources, the preparation of the annual estimates and subsequent management of the approved budget, operation of pay services for military personnel, and management engineering services, including automation. The comptroller general's branch is divided into three divisions, each headed by a director general. These are: director general finance, director general organization and manpower control, director general management engineering and automation.
In addition to the military branches of the Canadian forces headquarters, the civilian or administrative component of the department, under the direction of the deputy minister, was reorganized to correspond more closely with the organization of the military. The deputy minister's staff had been organized primarily on a functional basis for many years so the modifications were relatively minor. Prior to integration there had been four assistant deputy ministers responsible respectively for finance, personnel, requirements and construction. The functions of the last two offcials were merged to form a new position of assistant deputy minister (logistics). Inspection services was transferred from the jurisdiction of the deputy minister to materiel command while the deputy minister assumed control of the integrated directorate of infor-
[Mr. Hellyer.)

mation services and the audit functions previously performed by the services.
As mentioned earlier, the Defence Research Board was conceived and organized to provide a single agency responsible for defence research and for co-ordinating the military development programs. With the move toward unification, the military development programs were consolidated under the chief of technical services and the Defence Research Board's interest was maintained by integrating a number of defence scientists within the technical branch. Prior to 1965 there had been a directorate of scientific intelligence responsible to the chairman, Defence Research Board, and with the formation of an integrated director general of intelligence this directorate was absorbed. Apart from these changes, the operation of the research establishments has been unaffected, although some modifications in channels of communication between the Defence Research Board and the Canadian forces has, of course, become necessary.
It was pointed out to the 1964 special committee on defence that the defence council would be revitalized and used in a much more comprehensive way as the principal departmental policy group. The Minister of National Defence is the chairman of the defence council and the Associate Minister the vice-chairman. Other members are the chief of the defence staff, the vice-chief of the defence staff, the chairman of the defence research board and the deputy minister. It has become the practice to have the branch heads attend meetings of defence council regularly as well as some assistant deputy ministers. The deliberations, therefore, of members and those in attendance provide a valuable blending of military, scientific and financial advice.
The elements for a more co-ordinated, interdepartmental approach to defence problems exist in the defence council and consequently arrangements have been made for participation by representatives of other government departments on issues of interest to them. A senior officer of the Department of External Affairs attends regularly and this has proved to be a valuable link with that department. It is also a clear indication of our determination to ensure that Canadian defence policy is based upon and is designed to support Canadian foreign policy.

The role of the defence council forecast in 1964 has been fulfilled during the whole period of detailed planning on the unification process and this body has in fact become an active and decisive forum for the formulation of policy.
In the 29 months since defence council was reactivated in July, 1964, it has had 90 meetings dealing with matters covering the whole range of defence policy. For the 29 months preceding July, 1964, it met on four occasions.
As forecast in the white paper on defence (1964), the defence staff appointed in August, 1964, was given the responsibility of preparing plans and recommendations on the makeup of the field formations. The purpose was to develop a field command structure which would be suitable for the roles outlined for the Canadian forces in the white paper. After intensive study, the new integrated command structure was announced in June, 1965. The field commanders were appointed and command headquarters were established to organize the functional commands. The Canadian formations in Europe, the 4th Canadian Infantry Brigade Group, with headquarters at Soest, and 1 Air Division with headquarters at Metz, were not initially affected by the reorganization but the number of commands in Canada was reduced from 11 to six: mobile, maritime, air defence, air transport, materiel and training. The roles of these formations and commands will indicate how they fit into the integrated structure.
Our air division in Europe consists of eight CF-104 Star fighter squadrons. Six of the squadrons are located in Germany in a nuclear-strike role but have also been given a conventional bombing capability. The remaining two squadrons are located in France and have a reconnaissance role. As announced earlier this year, the two reconnaissance squadrons will be moved out of France during 1967. The number of squadrons will be reduced to six, four of them strike squadrons and two reconnaissance.
The outstanding performance of our ground and air crews with the air division has been and continues to be a matter of pride to all Canadians. As I told the standing committee on defence in May, it is not an exaggeration to say they are unmatched in the European
National Defence Act Amendment theatre, as evidenced by their consistent winning of air firing and air bombing trophies.
Our other outstanding formation in Europe is the 4th Canadian Infantry Brigade Group in Germany. Its operational capability has been greatly increased during the past two years with the acquisition of new weapons and equipment, including armoured personnel carriers, command post vehicles, tracked cargo vehicles, mortars, anti-tank missiles and communications equipment. Its fire power will be further increased in 1968 when the brigade's artillery regiment will be equipped with 155 millimetre self-propelled howitzers.
For its currently assigned role in the central European front the brigade group has today far greater fire power, mobility and protection than at any time since its formation. Man for man it is unsurpassed by any other unit in NATO.
Mobile command, which now has its headquarters at St. Hubert, P.Q., was established on October 1, 1965, with temporary headquarters in Longueuil, just outside Montreal.
Mobile command's mission is to maintain combat-ready land and tactical air forces capable of rapid deployment in circumstances ranging from service in the European theatre to United Nations and other peacekeeping operations. It is responsible for the provision of a rotational brigade for the land forces assigned to NATO in Europe, and for the training of two additional air-portable brigades designed for rapid deployment. The command is also forming the Canadian airborne regiment whose personnel and equipment can be rapidly sent to danger zones.
A vital component of mobile command is its tactical air element, and current planning calls for the formation of four squadrons of CF-5 tactical ground support aircraft. This includes the training squadron which will be formed in mid-1968, with the remaining squadrons being formed during the following 18 months. In addition to the formation of the CF-5 squadrons, plans are in hand for units of Buffalo transport aircraft and light and heavy helicopters to meet the need for air mobility in any combat zone. Studies are under way to produce even greater tactical air mobility and support for this important command.
As with the brigade group in Europe the field force elements assigned to mobile command are being re-equipped. In the past two
December 7, 1966

National Defence Act Amendment years this includes acquisition of armoured personnel carriers, command post vehicles, tracked cargo vehicles; new mortars, anti-tank missiles and communications equipment. Planning for the next five years envisions a continuing program of re-equipping which includes the acquisition of a new reconnaissance vehicle, the self-propelled 155 millimetre howitzers previously announced, vehicles with an over-snow and muskeg capability and a new light artillery weapon.

All maritime forces, both sea and air, came under this command which was created formally on January 17, 1966. With the exception of personnel in the functions taken over by training command and materiel command, maritime command includes the former Atlantic and Pacific commands of the Royal Canadian Navy, the former R.C.A.F. maritime air command and the former Atlantic and Pacific integrated maritime headquarters. Maritime headquarters is in Halifax and there is a Pacific sub-command in Esquimalt.
While the prime role of maritime command will continue to be anti-submarine warfare, planning is under way to increase its capability for general-purpose tasks. The capability of our maritime forces in both their primary and supporting roles will steadily improve as our modernization and shipbuilding program continues.
Our anti-submarine fleet is headed by the aircraft carrier Bonaventure which is now undergoing a major half-life refit and modernization. H.M.C.S. Fraser, the last of the St. Laurent class destroyers to undergo conversion to helicopter-destroyer status, rejoined the fleet in October of this year. This completes the refit and conversion program of the seven destroyers of this class. All are now manned and serving on the Atlantic coast and have been fitted with hangar and flight-deck facilities to operate the large Sea King antisubmarine helicopters, although some work is yet to be completed. Each has been equipped with the Canadian-developed variable depth sonar.
With the St. Laurent class there are now in commission nine helicopter-destroyers, including Nipigon and Annapolis, for which helicopter operations and variable depth sonar facilities were provided during construction.
The anti-submarine capability of these warships, which are included in the 20 destroyers built for the R.C.N. since the second world

war, is considered among the best in the world. The addition of the operational support ship Provider has increased this capability. The Provider, the largest ship ever built in Canada for the navy, is designed to support anti-submarine ships with fuel and supplies enabling them to remain on task for longer periods-in the order of two or three times, depending on the size of the force and the distance from harbour.
Two additional operational support ships are now planned to support maritime command's role. The operational support ships have a sea-lift capability and will be able to embark and discharge land vehicles and helicopters, and carry troops accompanying the vehicles, as well as accommodating personnel landing craft.
The fleet's anti-submarine capability is to be further increased through the modernization program for the seven Restigouche class destroyer escorts. This modernization will incorporate improved detection systems and the ASROC anti-submarine weapon system. These improvements, together with the much improved torpedoes being procured for all ships, will about double their present detection range and add a greatly improved "kill" capability.
New construction also includes four helicopter-destroyers which will be primarily anti-submarine vessels but with secondary capabilities of gun fire and reconnaissance support of landing operations and engagement of light surface forces with gun fire. These helicopter-destroyers will include the Canadian Sea Sparrow in their armament. This is an all-weather, close range surface-to-air missile system which will also be fitted in the two new operational support ships for defence against air attack. The first of the new helicopter-destroyers is planned for delivery in late 1970.
The surface fleet is supported by three older destroyers held in reserve. Two of these, Algonquin and Crescent, were modernized in the 1950's.
In addition, six minesweepers, four harbour defence ships and three patrol boats are in reserve; it is planned to use some of these as training ships.
One Oberon class submarine has joined the fleet and two others are under construction in England and will join in the next two years. Although these are used for training of the

maritime forces in peacetime, they, nevertheless, are credited with a good anti-submarine capability. The submarine Grilse is on the west coast.
In addition to the operational support ship Provider, the force is supported by the mobile support ship Cape Scott. On the west coast the mobile support ship Cape Breton is in reserve.
A vital component of maritime command are the six air squadrons which carry out far-ranging surveillance tasks off Canada's coasts. These squadrons consist of three equipped with the long-range Argus which ranks as high as any long-range maritime air craft in use in the world today. The fourth is equipped with the Neptune, the fifth has Tracker aircraft and the sixth Sea King helicopters. The latter two operate from the aircraft carrier Bonaventure, and the Sea Kings also operate from helicopter-destroyers. The Argus, Neptune and Tracker training units provide additional operational capability which is available for an emergency.
The air component of maritime command will be further enhanced as the Argus and Trackers are fitted with improved anti-submarine and communications equipment. These improvements and additions to our maritime forces will assure the continued readiness of maritime command to carry out its mission.
The naval share of the current five-year equipment and equipment development program, ending March 31, 1971, is approximately $460 million. This represents a 23 per cent increase in the navy's share in equipment and equipment development over that spent in the previous five years.
In recognition of our commitment to North American Air Defence Command (NORAD), the role of air defence command is to contribute to defence of our continent in concert with forces of the United States. The operations of the command were not affected significantly by the integration process. The command employs the CF101 Voodoo interceptor and the Bomarc surface to air missile and operates a number of radars and a space surveillance device in support of its role. Economies of operation have been achieved through the merger of the command headquarters with northern NORAD region headquarters at North Bay.
The personnel of this command continue to carry out their assigned missions in support of North American air defence in a first-class
National Defence Act Amendment manner. As Air Commodore A. C. Hull, then the acting commander of air defence command, stated before the standing committee on national defence on June 28, 1966:
We met or exceeded all assigned objectives ot operational effectivenes by a progressive schedule of inspections and evaluations, tactical evaluations, alert force capability tests, nuclear capability tests and the emergency defence plan tests-
Training command headquarters was formed in Winnipeg on January 1, 1966, and is respons.ble for individual training, including flying and trades training, for all personnel in the Canadian forces. It is not, however, responsible for unit or operational training.
The training program being developed will take some years to become fully effective. It is being designed, for the non-commissioned ranks, to correspond with the new trades structure recently announced for the forces. Training will be conducted to meet basic requirements in both operational and technical skills. Where skills are common to two or three environments the training will be centralized; other training will be given at schools that are oriented toward a particular environment. This centralization will result in more rational employment of instructors and avoid multiplicity of facilities and equipment. As an important by-product it will provide the base for the development of common doctrine for common skills throughout the service.
Air transport command's primary role is to provide the department with a strategic airlift capability. Although this role was not changed with integration, there has been a shift in emphasis toward the troop-carrier mission, and a marked improvement in the capacity of this command to take into account in its planning and operations the full range of air transport needs of the forces as a whole.
As stated to the standing committee on national defence during a briefing on June 16, 1966, under the auspices of Air Commodore G. G. Diamond, commander of air transport command:
Air transport command's operating standards are unsurpassed by any similar military air transport organization in the world.
I am sure that all hon. members who have flown with this command would strongly endorse this conclusion.
The command operates Yukon and Hercules turbo-prop aircraft as its major long range

National Defence Act Amendment carriers, and a variety of smaller aircraft for tactical air transport, communications, search and rescue and reserve training. The fleet of Hercules aircraft has markedly improved the command's support capability. A new medium-range jet transport, the Falcon, has also been ordered.

We are studying our possible requirements for the future and are keeping abreast of developments in the air transport field with a view to modernizing our fleet when it becomes timely to do so.
Materiel command was created on August 1, 1965, with headquarters in Rockcliffe, Ontario.
The main aim or mission of the command is to provide the necessary supply and maintenance support to the other functional commands.
Materiel command was presented with one of the most formidable tasks in the integration program. Over the years, the three services had each developed different supply systems. It is materiel command's job to mould them into a single automated supply system. Planning is well advanced for the new system and a number of steps have already been taken. Two examples are the integrating of the cataloguing function and the amalgamation of staffs and services required below command headquarters level to administer and support depots in a particular locality.
Because of the complexity and magnitude of the project, however, it will take from three to five years to implement fully the single automated system. In the meantime, the three existing systems are being operated by materiel command and the logistic support to the forces has not in any way been diminished.
As a participant in every United Nations peacekeeping action since the organization was formed, Canada has made and continues to make a substantial contribution to world order through such operations.
At the present time there are more than 1,900 Canadian officers and men serving the United Nations and the International Control Commission in countries around the world. In Cyprus, 900 servicemen form a key part in that U.N. peacekeeping force. In the Suez, a

I have first-hand knowledge of the splendid work these Canadians are doing and I think all Canada should be proud of their efforts.
The long record of Canada's participation toward the maintenance of world peace includes such other places as Palestine, Kashmir, Lebanon, the Congo, West New Guinea, Yemen, the India-Pakistan border and Indochina. In the latter area, Canada has been a member of the International Commission for Supervision and Control since 1954 and at present we have 65 officers and men on duty there. Our capability to provide such forces for UN type operations is not only being maintained, but with the emphasis we are placing on increased mobility and flexibility, it is steadily being increased.
Although not a command, the Canadian forces communications system has functional responsibilities throughout the Canadian forces. The role of the system is to provide strategic communications for the forces and for emergency government. It is not responsible for tactical communications, such as ship-to-shore, tactical air-ground-air and field communications which are organic to combat commands.
The Canadian forces communications system was implemented by forming a small headquarters in Ottawa, but not part of Canadian forces headquarters, utilizing staffs formerly responsible for the three separate service strategic communications networks. During the 18 months to date of its existence, the system has realized many of the improvements and economies to be expected under a single management.
Almost coincident with the formation of the Canadian forces communications system, a comprehensive two-year study began of all Department of National Defence non-tactical communications. A team of consultants from the CN/CP Telecommunications organization was engaged to develop a long-range phased plan for the augmentation and automation of the communications operated by the system.
Through consolidation and automation of the many manually-operated and largely obsolescent centres now in the Canadian forces
December 7, 1966	COMMONS
communications system, substantial savings in personnel can be expected, along with greatly increased speed and quality of communications. The major re-equipping programs arising from this study will begin about 1970. At this time, the Canadian armed forces will be provided with vastly improved, modern strategic communications befitting a first-class military organization.
In order to provide an effective two-way flow of information -between Canadian forces headquarters and the major commands, the Canadian forces council was formed as an advisory body to the chief of the defence staff and has been meeting at regular intervals since August, 1966. This council makes available to the chief of the defence staff the advice and opinions of the senior commanders. It not only increases the timely flow of information between these two top echelons of command but, in addition, provides a means of utilizing the wealth of ideas and expertise which exists at all levels throughout the forces.
Thus we have a system which not only acquaints all commanders with the major activities of their counterparts but also gives each of the commanders knowledge of important matters under consideration at C.F.H.Q. A regular means of consultation has been established enabling field commanders to contribute to the decision-making process.
The Canadian forces council meets once a month in Ottawa and is attended by the chief and vice-chief of the defence staff, the deputy minister, the chairman of the Defence Research Board, the three branch heads, the deputy chief for reserves, the secretary of the defence staff and the commanders of the six major commands. Other commanders from formations outside Canada may also attend from time to time.
The aim of the reorganization of the Canadian forces was clearly stated in the white paper and is intended to achieve certain specific and well-defined goals. After referring to the companion problems of an effective command system and growing overhead costs, future policy was outlined in unmistakable terms:
Following the most careful and thoughtful consideration, the government has decided that there is only one adequate solution. It is the integration of the armed forces of Canada under a single chief of defence staff. This will be the first step toward a single unified defence force for Canada.
National Defence Act Amendment
This was reiterated in a circular letter issued jointly by myself and the associate minister to all members of the armed forces and civilian employees of the Department of National Defence on April 2, 1964. This letter said, in part:
The third and final step will be the unification of the three services. . . It is reasonable to expect that it will be three or four years before it will be possible to take this action.
We also stated in the next paragraph:
However, the end objective of a single service is firm.
The point was again made in testimony before the special committee on defence on May 28, 1964, when I said:
far as the ultimate objective is concerned this has been clearly stated in the white paper, and I think this is a fair recognition that this is the first step towards a single unified force for Canada.
It was also emphasized repeatedly in various statements that the changes in Canada's defence organization would take place step by step. Unification is the end objective of a logical and evolutionary progression. Although integration and unification are sometimes regarded as alternatives, and inherently different, they are, in fact, merely different stages in the same process. Integration was actually the term applied to the first stages of the unification of the Canadian armed forces.

In the reorganization of the Canadian forces after world war II, the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force were continued as separate service components of the Canadian forces. Each was provided with a chief of staff who, under the law, was given responsibility for the control and administration of the service which he headed. This continued each service as an entity within the Canadian forces with all of the necessary headquarters, command, training, support and operational machinery for each. In the course of time, the efficiency and the economics of operating on this basis came more and more into question. Elaborate machinery was devised to co-ordinate the planning and operations as well as various aspects of the administration of the three services. A good deal was accomplished through joint planning, by assigning support responsibilities in some instances to one service, by integrating services in a few cases, by inter-service committees and other forms of consultation. Nevertheless, the surface had barely been
10828	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment scratched and the full potential was beyond reach by means that were consistent with maintaining the services as separate entities. When the decision was taken in 1964 to abolish the chiefs of staff of the three individual services and head the Canadian forces by a single chief of staff, it meant that the three services would no longer retain their status as individual entities within the Canadian forces.

Control and administration were transferred to a single chief of staff and this resulted, as was intended, in a single planning, management, administrative, training and support process. The concept of three separate service entities was thereby abandoned in favour of one.
Comprehension of the concept of a single service will be assisted by an understanding of the structure of the force. The headquarters and command structure, having been integrated, are now organized for all practicable purposes on a single service basis.
Canadian forces headquarters gives direction and provides headquarters services across the whole spectrum of defence and is responsible for readjustment of command responsibilities and resources should an operational situation require it. This is a direct single line responsibility.
The force structure is comprised of force units which may be used individually or in combination depending on the military tasks to be undertaken. These force units are the infantry companies, the armoured squadrons, the artillery batteries, the engineering squadrons, field ambulances, the air squadrons, warships and the support ships, to mention a few. None of these will be changed in moving to a single service from three separate services. They will continue to be trained and equipped for their particular roles. Moreover, a single service will involve no change in the organization of these force units into formations such as brigades, air wings, or squadrons of ships. On the other hand, the deployment of these units and formations is directed by a single command chain in accordance with the missions assigned, and under a single command responsible for these missions.
The concept of a single service does raise questions of identity-those of the spirit, motivation and esprit de corps-which are difficult to measure objectively but which are nevertheless so very important in a military force. It would be surprising if men who had

DEBATES	December 7, 1966
been associated and identified with the individual services did not encounter some difficulty in the realignment of loyalties involved in the establishment of a single service. Most of us have experienced similar problems in the course of our lifetime as institutions to which we have become deeply committed have had to change, and none of us would underestimate the soul-searching readjustments that are necessary. Within the single service we will continue to have intense loyalties to the fighting units and broader associations within it. This has been demonstrated most clearly in the past within the Canadian Army with its regiments and corps. Here the officers and men have generated the pride, loyalties and qualities that have won both for their regiment and corps and for the Canadian Army as a whole outstanding reputations. The organization of the Royal Canadian Navy and Royal Canadian Air Force has tended toward identification with the service as a whole, but we are all aware of the great pride members of these services took in the achievements of the ships and squadrons and other units to which they belonged.
In the single service these important relationships within the total force will continue and will foster the same kind of esprit de corps as there has been in the past. It is none the less important that a sense of purpose and a sense of belonging to one single service, covering all aspects of defence and designed to tackle the complex defence problems of the future, be developed. The band of brothers must take in the whole family and be one family although there will be many spirited, competitive but mutually supporting groups of brothers within it. One force, with one name, a common uniform, and common rank designations will nurture this total family loyalty.
With this background as to what is meant by unification, that is, the creation of a single service absorbing the present three, I wish to discuss in more detail some of the advantages in taking this step.
The principle of the bill to create a single service is very simple. It is to permit the personnel, officers and men, and the units already subject to unified control and management, to be held in one entity rather than three. There are four fundamental reasons why this is considered to be desirable for the service, the serviceman and Canada:
December 7, 19B6
With the establishment of a common identity, sailors, soldiers and airmen, although loyal to their ships, regiments and squadrons, will have an overriding loyalty to the whole force and its total objectives on behalf of Canada.
For able and highly motivated individuals, both officers and other ranks, wider, more challenging and rewarding career opportunities will be available.
The unified force will provide much greater flexibility to meet changing requirements in defence organization made necessary by advances in military technology and changes in the international situation.
The nature of modern warfare has resulted in a compaction of time and distance to the point where decision-making and reaction time must be much swifter than ever before in history. A unified force best meets this demand.
I would like to elaborate on each of these points. The first is of significant importance.
As I mentioned previously it has always been and will remain important to feel a strong loyalty to one's unit, formation or command. The world, however, has become so complex due to rapid technological changes that modern military operations have become increasingly interdependent. The old recognizable deviding lines between land, sea and air have long since disappeared. Therefore it has become imperative that there be a higher loyalty beyond that which is given to a particular service.
More and more military tasks can now be carried out by any one of the three traditional services. For purposes of illustration only let us consider the example of the nuclear-strike role under NATO which is now performed for Canada by manned aircraft of the Royal Canadian Air Force. This role could be performed in substance by (1) land-based missiles; (2) missiles launched from surface ships or submarines; (3) another type of manned aircraft,
This means that there are three possible options: land, sea or air-at present army, navy or air force. Under the three-service system it is almost certain that the service currently assigned to the role will recommend a weapon system traditional to that service.
National Defence Act Amendment
Modern operations analysis seeks to compare the potential effectiveness of different techniques in relation to the resources available. In order to get the best results from this kind of analysis, however, it is necessary to employ the most objective judgment, first in setting our criteria for the analysis and secondly in interpreting the results of the analysis.
This is one area where a single service bias can produce, and historically has often produced, a result which is not the most effective in relation to the cost. The more objectivity that can be applied to the studies the better the chances of the right solution. It would be impossible to eliminate all bias because individuals will naturally be influenced by their own specialized training and background. If their higher loyalty, however, is to the force as a whole, rather than to one of the traditional three services, the probability of reaching logical conclusions will be greatly increased.
Another problem in relation to identity, which is solved by unification, is that of job quotas or representation by service. As long as there are three separate services each one demands its share of available positions. This applies to some extent in the commands and to a very large extent in headquarters at all levels. There are, of course, some positions where special skill and particular professional training are required. There are, however, very large numbers of staff positions which can well be filled by officers coming from any one of a number of military specialties, and where the job should go to the best man available, regardless of his earlier specialty. Some rotation may be desirable but it should not be the overriding factor. The most important consideration should be the appointment of the best qualified person available for the job.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Unification will provide better and fairer employment prospects for service personnel. Under a system of separate services, opportunities are naturally limited to the scope, tasks and requirements of the individual service. An integrated command structure provides some additional outlet, but this is limited, normally, to the senior management level as opposed to the broad opportunities and advantages presented by a single service.
