National Defence Act Amendment
Another facet of career prospects is the improvement of promotion opportunities for the abler personnel. From a broader base of selection it will be possible to identify, develop and appoint the best qualified to the more senior ranks. Artificial barriers created by three separate services and the need for representation on staffs by service will be eliminated. Standardized career planning under unification will afford improved opportunity. The challenges and opportunities for the gifted individual will be much greater than could ever be possible in a system of separate services.
In the post-war period many administrative regulations have been issued to achieve equality in the treatment of service personnel. However, there are many aspects of personnel administration where differences have continued as a result of variations in individual service policies. As integration proceeded and people from different services worked side by side, the differences between the forces came into the open and more and more into question. Without attempting a complete listing, some of the differences that have come to light are worth noting:
1.	Inequities in promotion opportunities among officers and men in the same general trades by reason of different approaches among the services in the use of trade and rank.
2.	Inequities in opportunity for men to reach commissioned rank. Each service has its own set of stipulations for men to be considered for promotion to commissioned status. These differences could well result in the least qualified of three persons, in the three separate services, being commissioned in a particular trade which in essence, was common to all services.
3.	Inequities in the opportunity for in-service education to suitable young men in the ranks to qualify them for entry into the officer candidate programs. The navy was the only service which had a formal in-service academic training program for this purpose.
4.	Inequities in trades training. In the Royal Canadian Air Force solid basic training has been given with subsequent advancement through on-the-job training. On the other hand the Royal Canadian Navy and the Canadian Army require men at most trade levels to undergo a formal trade course to qualify for the next trade level. This has had the effect of differing opportunities for trade advancement.

DEBATES	December 7, 1966
Differences in trade and other standards necessary to qualify for promotion have given rise to some cases of men in the same trade working together in integrated establishments in which less qualified men from one service have been promoted before men from another service. Almost 20 years of post-war effort through inter-service committees and other means failed to bring about equitable conditions of service for servicemen. Integration had the effect of vividly exposing these differences. In the course of time many of them could be dealt with by the integrated staffs. On the other hand, there are limitations imposed by the existence of three separate legal entities. These will be overcome by the creation of one service.
The trade or occupational structure varied from one service to another, and the conditions for extra pay based on skill were not always the same. This was the case even though the whole question of standardizing the occupational classes in the services had been receiving attention through virtually the whole of the post-war period. Since 1964, under the stimulus of integration, much has been accomplished. The first step, which is essential for efficiency, was to identify all those who perform similar functions and to group them together. This required an occupational analysis which in the case of some classes offered little difficulty. In other occupational fields, the technical and specialized nature of the work makes the classification of people more difficult. The result of the classification work directed by the integrated headquarters has been the rationalization of more than 300 occupational classes to approximately 100. One invaluable result has been to recognize for the first time the commonality that exists across the services.
A personnel structure has been developed for officers and men in the unified service. The same general principles have been applied to achieve appropriate groupings for the purpose of personnel management and professional development. These unified structures will open to personnel of all ranks wider opportunities for the development and employment of their skills and professional talent. A unified service will permit them to advance across old services barriers and so provide greater avenues for service and greater opportunities for personal advancement. When people are able to move in a broad stream, which does not confine employment opportunities to narrow specialities or to the individual naval, army or air force entities, both the individual and the force as a whole will clearly benefit.
December 7, 196S	COMMONS
It should not be forgotten that requirements for tradesmen and other personnel with particular skills will obviously vary as new weapons systems are introduced or as updated procedures are adopted. In some cases this will mean that trained people will have to be transferred to other occupational classes. Where this is essential for the efficient management of the services, there can be no alternative but to do it, although the interests of the individual concerned must be safeguarded. Such adjustments will, we believe, be much more easily accomplished when the alternative opportunities are not limited, as they have been in the past, to one service.
The services individually can offer interesting, challenging and rewarding careers to Canadian youth. The opportunities will be multiplied when the services are unified. This is important if we are to attract and retain the high standard of applicants in the numbers needed to meet the challenges of the modern Canadian forces.	.
One general principle should be underlined again. The combat units will retain their identity, and their specialized functions and training. It is important to state that it is not and never has been any part of the planning associated with unification to convert our servicemen to "jacks-of-all-trades".

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
An infantry soldier will not be asked to do the job of a sailor in a fighting ship; a sailor will not be asked to fight in an infantry platoon; and a fighter pilot will not be required to drive a tank.
Nothing has had a more profound influence on the character of modern military operations than the post-war scientific and technological advances in both weaponry and delivery systems. The influence of these advances on strategic concepts and the conduct of international relations has been revolutionary. Rather than dwell on the intercontinental or global aspects of technological change, I would like to focus attention on its impact on service roles.
Many of these developments cut across the traditional lines of distinction between the different services. One example of this is the anti-submarine warfare equipment which can be carried in land-based aircraft or carrier-based aircraft, or in ships on or under the sea. Another example is the use in all three services of fixed-wing aircraft and missiles. Still
National Defence Act Amendment another is the use of helicopters in all three armed forces as reconnaissance vehicles, weapons platforms and instruments of mobility. The recent creation by the United States of mobile divisions with their reliance on helicopters may mark a departure from tradition which will have a profound influence on the nature of military activities. There are numerous other such examples. Suffice it to say the problems associated with the assignment of responsibilities for these and many other weapons systems, such as missiles and rockets, are well recognized.
Such changes must affect the organization of the forces. It is clear that the influence works in the direction of a single service for reasons of military effectiveness, cost and career considerations.
A unified force permits a much more objective analysis to be made of the most desirable way in which to employ weapons systems. Unification will enhance our ability to react to changing requirements. Our adaptability to changes in weapons technology and in the international situation will be much greater when the artificial barriers, imposed by having personnel divided into three legal entities rather than one, are removed. Unification will broaden the opportunities available to service motivated and expensively trained personnel when changes in roles or systems alter requirements. In this way, the nation will benefit, the force as a whole will benefit, and. just as important, the serviceman himself will benefit.	[DOT]
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The white paper of 1964 would not have recommended integration as a first step toward a single service if we had not been certain of the improved capacity of a unified force to meet the demands of modern warfare. The pattern of warfare in which armies fought armies, navies fought navies, and air forces fought air forces is not likely to be repeated. Under the traditional three service concept, the individual service recruited, administered, trained, equipped and supported the combat force units within that service. Joint or combined headquarters were created, where necessary, to co-ordinate and direct the operations of the elements of two or more of the services. This is a device necessary in a three-service system, but it has built-in drawbacks arising out of the very fact that units and elements belong to different services. Each component depends on its parent service
December 7, 1866

National Defence Act Amendment for support in a host of ways which require special channels of communication and complex methods of co-ordination throughout.
Commanders and staff down to the lowest level of operations, and in the support echelons from the scene of operations back to the home base, must act together and in unison as the situation demands. Under conditions of modern warfare consultation between services, having different areas of responsibility and different channels of communication is time consuming. More important, it cannot achieve the high degree of co-ordinated response that could be critical and would be immediately available through a single organization. The old system can result in misunderstanding and delay which, at best, a military activity can ill afford and, under some circumstances, it could not afford at all.
The need for fast decision-making and quick reaction is synonymous with modem warfare. The introduction of jets, missiles, rockets, computers, satellite reconnaissance vehicles and many other new military techniques demands an expeditious resolution of problems and rapid response. For intercontinental warfare, the impact of the contraction of time and distance is quite evident. But it is also valid in relation to military activities at the lower end of the spectrum. Even the success or failure of peace-restoring or peacekeeping operations can well depend on the speed with which decisions are reached and the force and its equipment delivered to the trouble zone.
I believe it is a fair conclusion that a single organization which works and thinks together day in and day out, with direct lines of communication and a single line of responsibility, eliminates the self-inflicted problems associated with the three service system of coordinating combined operations.
There are clearly customs and traditions in any institution that are very valuable and which ought to be preserved if at all possible. Unification of the Canadian forces does not imply the abandonment of tradition, of pride in the unit and other ingredients of esprit de corps. The preservation of the intangible factors which support and sustain any fighting unit is an essential goal but along with this it is important to foster innovation. The stimulus of new ideas and methods injects enthusiasm and vigour into any organization.

Morale is related not just to the glories gone by but equally or even more to the importance of the job to be done and the effectiveness of the leadership, training and equipment to do the job well. People including military personnel, like to feel that what they are doing is worth while, is in the public interest and is recognized as such. The development of clearly defined roles, the provision of better equipment to carry out those roles, and the anticipated public recognition of the efficient and useful defence concept being developed should have a beneficial effect on the morale of service personnel in the unified force.

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext: What will it do with the people?

subtopic: AMALGAMATION OF NAVY, ARMY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
They will have the added satisfaction of knowing that they are setting the pace for the world in modernizing the organization of military forces.
Unification will result in a single service not abandoning but building upon traditions of the past and injecting that enthusiasm and vigour required for a dynamic new organization.
The Canadian forces now consist by law of three services, the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force. The respect which each of these services enjoys today has been earned in peace and in war. Members of this house know the history. It has been recorded by many eminent Canadian writers. But more enduringly it has been recorded in blood, in sorrow and in gratitude embedded in the hearts of Canadians and in the hearts of our friends in other lands whose freedom and dignity have been restored and preserved by Canada's sailors, soldiers and airmen.
The three services under the provisions of the bill become one service to be called the Canadian Armed Forces. It is understandable that proud and gallant men may read this with heavy hearts. Those who do, I hope, will on reflection see that the single service is born with the great heritages of the three services that give it its life blood. These are not lost but brought together into one service, the strength of three to meet the challenges of the future and to add to the glories of the past.
The name of the single service "The Canadian Armed Forces" was chosen after the
December 7, 19GG	COMMONS
most careful and thoughtful consideration by the defence staff. Since there is no noun which describes the single service, it is necessary to either invent a new word or adopt existing words and change their meaning to include all armed forces, whether for sea, land, air or space. After exhaustive study within the services, the defence staff recommended that the name of the single service should be the Canadian Armed Forces. It is possible that a word will be coined at some future date which will apply to servicemen of all environments and should this be the case, it can be adopted by a simple amendment.
In choosing the name Canadian Armed Forces, consideration was given to the question of the Royal title. In the three services two different systems were used. In the army, the Royal title was applied at the corps and regimental levels while in the navy and air force it was applied in the name of the service itself. After careful study the defence staff recommended that the former system be adopted. As new groupings and associations are developed in the Canadian Armed Forces the members, through the defence staff, may seek the use of the Royal prefix in the new names selected. This would be consistent with the system adopted.
Permission to use the Royal title is of course a prerogative of Her Majesty. When the Royal Canadian Navy was established in 1910 as the Canadian Naval Service and when the Royal Canadian Air Force was first organized in 1920 as the Canadian Air Force, "Royal" was not included in the names. This came later and reflected a wish of the members of those services to be so designated. I feel strongly that this is a matter which should be influenced largely by the wishes of the members of the Canadian Armed Forces and that, in the course of time, a consensus will develop. An imposed decision at this time would neither be wise nor, from information at hand, be welcomed by the members of the forces.

speechtext:
Members of the navy, the army and the air force will become members of the Canadian Armed Forces when the relevant section of the bill comes into force. Before this happens, however, all members of the forces will be provided with full information on conditions of service which will apply to them in the
National Defence Act Amendment unified service. It will take some time to complete the details after the bill has been enacted by parliament. This section of the bill will not, therefore, be brought into force for some time-probably several months. Consultation will continue with functional commanders as details are worked out.
Present members of the forces will be guaranteed under the provisions of the bill that they will not be required to perform duty they could not have been required to perform in the service to which they belonged. Because of this commitment, no special provisions on retirement benefits are required.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
As the question of pension penalty has been referred to from time to time in previous discussions, I would like to clarify this. The so-called "pension penalty" is in fact not a penalty but an actuarial adjustment that is made for early retirement at the member's request. The pension in these circumstances is paid over a longer period of time. This is a standard arrangement in almost all pension plans, civilian and military, and there is no justification for changing it. The same reasoning applies to other obligations which may apply to the service of some members, such as the obligation to serve for a specified number of years following completion of a post-graduate course at service expense or, if retirement is accepted, the obligation to refund all or part of the cost. Such obligations will continue to apply.
The emphasis in this reorganization is on equitable and reasonable treatment for those who are already members of the Canadian forces. The roles for those who, in future, enroll in the unified force also should be stated. Men and women who decide to join the Canadian Armed Forces will have a wide selection of interesting employment and if they are qualified, and vacancies are available, they will be offered the employment of their preference. If they join, it normally will be for an initial engagement of five years. If this engagement is mutually satisfactory, they may, under the provisions of the bill, be reengaged for an indefinite period. If they want to be released later, this can be done with six months notice, except in an emergency or during periods of obligatory service.
This proposed new concept of one engagement followed by an indefinite period of service has been described as the "career serviceman concept". It is one of the imaginative recommendations contained in the report of a
10834	COMMONS
National Defence Act Amendment military manpower study conducted by the services. This concept will allow us to do away with a good deal od administration involved in the periodic re-engagement procedure and, more important, will allow us to place non-commissioned ranks on the same professional footing as commissioned officers in the service. It does one more thing: it provides a definite point in time, after five years of service, when both the service and the individual make up their minds about his career in the service.
. The present law provides that the Royal Canadian Navy, the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force shall be comprised of such units and other elements as are from time to time organized by or under authority of the minister. In the bill the same authority is provided in respect of the Canadian Armed Forces. At the time the new force comes into being, its units and elements shall be those which then exist in the navy, army and air force.
Units and elements of the force are the command entities-for example, in the navy, ships and squadrons; in the army, battalions of infantry, regiments of artillery, armoured regiments, brigades; in the air force, squadrons, wings and groups. All of these will remain unchanged.
The regimental framework of the land element is, in fact, groupings of officers and men with common professional interests. This system will not be changed by reason of unification. Certainly, we will continue to have infantry regiments as well as the Royal Canadian Armoured Corps and the Royal Regiment of Canadian Artillery. Others will change as they are amalgamated with similar groups in other services and new groupings will unquestionably be needed and desired for the new force. These will be made progressively as the need is made evident.
The time required to complete the reorganization of the forces will likely take some years but changes will be implemented progressively after proclamation of the bill as soon as each becomes practicable. Although a unified personnel management system will be introduced, the separate units and elements of naval, field and air forces will continue to exist. That is to say, while the barriers to movement of personnel between the forces will be removed, personnel in the combat forces will continue to be identified as sailors,

DEBATES	December 7, 1966
soldiers and airmen until the force structure within the unified force is developed.
Rank names are important and the selection of a single set does not yield to any easy or scientific solution. The decision to adopt as official the ranks indicated in the bill is based on the strong belief by the defence staff that they will be acceptable to the largest number of service people and will be most familiar to the Canadian public.
The associate minister and I realize that a sudden break with old rank designations would be difficult for some servicemen, particularly so for many members of the navy where there is a high degree of similarity of rank designations among navies with which they usually work. The bill would enable the minister to prescribe alternative titles of rank to those used officially for documentation, pay, etc., and state the circumstances under which they might be used. It is my intention to authorize members of the Canadian Armed Forces to use rank titles traditional to their former service. In the fullness of time, the defence staff and I expect the new rank titles to come into general use by preference of the members of the unified service.
Almost from the beginning of the discussion of the reorganization, there has been keen public interest in the uniforms which would be adopted under unification. This is understandable because of the symbolic and traditional importance of uniforms in any military force. I would like to state at this point what the present plans are.
Occupational clothing will continue to be worn in relation to specific employment as is now the case. For example, appropriate combat clothing will be worn by forces in the field, at sea and in the air.
A new service dress, to be worn by all ranks, will be introduced over a period of years. The same cloth will be used for officers and men. I strongly endorse the feeling of the defence staff that, in the modern forces Canada enjoys today with the high percentage of technically trained non-officers and the over-all high calibre of our men, it is no longer acceptable to have them wear anything but top-grade material and design of uniform. They are first-class; they should look first-class. Economies will be achieved over the long haul through bulk buying, reduced inventories and lower distribution costs. There will, of course,
December 7, 1966	COMMONS
be an initial capital outlay. To ensure that the uniform is the best procurable, the trials and developments of firm specifications will take time, and it is forecast that it may be anywhere from three to five years before the new uniform will be in general use. It is planned to introduce a small number of uniforms for trial purposes in the spring of next year but general issue will take place later. Appropriate insignia will be used to designate the environmental specialties of the servicemen but final recommendations concerning these insignia and the insignia of rank have not yet been made.
As it will take a considerable time to provide new uniforms for the Canadian Armed Forces, current uniforms will be used during the intervening period. Subsequently, members may continue to wear the present uniforms as dress uniforms on appropriate occasions. In this respect, these uniforms will be considered the equivalent of the army blue patrol.
The regiments of the army will be authorized to continue to wear regimental dress uniforms on appropriate occasions. The Royal Canadian Navy and the R.C.A.F. have no comparable order of dress but members of the three services may continue to wear their present mess dress.
The provisions of the bill also apply to the reserves which will be in a separate component of a single service in the same way that they have been separate components of the three services in the past.
The reserves were reorganized in 1964 with the object of improving their posture to meet their important and primary role supporting the regular forces. That role will continue into the indefinite future. As the composition of the regular force component of the single service is evolved, some complementary changes in the reserve component will no doubt be necessary. We do not propose, however, to make any changes at the outset but to continue the present organization within the framework of the single service.
The deputy chief reserves has been given the responsibility of ensuring that the interrelationships between the regular and reserve components are under continuous study in consultation with the officers of the reserves. Any changes that may eventually be made will be designed to strengthen the capacity of the reserves to support the regular component as changes are made in it. Our intention is to
National Defence Act Amendment ensure that the reserves have a meaningful task. In doing this, there will be full consultation with the conference of defence associations.
The cadet organizations are directed to the development of leadership, good citizenship, patriotism and an interest in the military affairs of our country among the youth. The Navy League of Canada, the Air Cadet League, the provincial departments of education and other organizations co-sponsor the cadet activities with the Department of National Defence. Much of the success of the movement is due to the untiring efforts of the interested civilians who support these organizations. No changes will be made except those considered advisable as a consequence of changes in the regular force after discussion with our partners in this enterprise. The deputy chief reserves has the responsibility to ensure that we in the Department of National Defence are fully responsive to the need of the cadet organizations as changes or modifications in present arrangements are necessary.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
As members study this bill, I am confident they will find that the changes proposed are of a reasonable nature. The object of this bill is not to destroy and erase at one stroke the traditions of the past but to build, on the solid foundation we have forged, a strong and viable force to meet Canada's needs of tomorrow. Those needs are not readily predictable in a rapidly changing world but it can be said with assurance that Canada's influence in the years ahead and its capacity to act in favour of peace and settlement of disputes that endanger peace will grow with its own development. Canada's military organization should not be circumscribed in any way, including inherited traditional means of organization, from developing into a force to best meet the demands that may be placed on it in the years ahead.
I believe that the present division into three separate service components imposes restrictions and that these barriers should be removed both in the interests of the most effective military forces for the future and in the interest of the men and women who belong to the force. That is the essence of this bill. It has nothing to do with the question of naval forces, land forces, air forces or even space forces. Rather, it has to do with the management, the strategic and operational
December 7, 1966

National Defence Act Amendment planning, the training and support, the capacity of the force to adjust to changing requirements, and the ability of the force to provide meaningful, challenging and rewarding careers for service personnel. All of these needs are enhanced by unification rather than the traditional separation of the men and women who comprise the force into three components.
Since August, 1964, when individuals have been drawn from the three services to man the integrated headquarters, commands and bases, it has become clear that service distinctions were no longer appropriate in the broad basis of integrated employment. This was particularly evident at the headquarters and in those commands whose missions extended beyond those associated with one service and where the need to maintain service distinctions complicated the operation rather than
helped it. This confirmed, if any confirmation was necessary, the validity of the original concept that integration was the first step in the unification cycle. It would become increasingly difficult to maintain in a satisfactory way the separation of the Canadian forces in three service components as required by law and, as much detailed work must be done to bring about a unified force, I consider it necessary to seek parliamentary approval now of the changes in the law that will provide the basis for this work to proceed.
I am confident that the establishment of a single unified defence force for Canada is right for the nation, right for the force as a whole and right for the men and women who serve and will serve in it.

Yesterday in his absence questions were asked in the first part of the question period concerning the situation and the reports which had been received in respect of the emergency. The initimation earlier today was that we would be asking the house later in the day to provide some means to deal with the emergency legislation.

The situation in the St. Lawrence river is a little different. Those ports are open. In the normal course of events, assuming the weather is similar to what it has been over the years, these ports will be open for some considerable time. Some of the ports may be closed because of weather conditions later on, although I believe last year shipping came into the harbours of that river in each month of the year. I could not agree that the situation in the St. Lawrence is one which requires emergency legislation. I could not ask the house to take that position. I would be less than truthful if I said there was legislation in respect of that subject available for consideration at this time by the house because there is not.
However, the implications of the tie-up of shipping on the west coast, having in mind the exports and imports involved and the tie-up in the four western provinces, are very great indeed. I do not propose to indicate the significance of this situation because I presume all hon. members appreciate its significance in relation to our export of food and other material, but I ask the hon. member for Lapointe, in light of the situation, to reconsider his position and acquiesce to the request that the house deal with this matter which is regarded by all Canadians as an emergency.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a special appeal to the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). The circumstances on the Pacific coast are extremely critical and, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) has pointed out, several thousand men have been thrown out of work. Perishable commodities should be loaded and unloaded and export contracts for the sale of wheat are being held up. Grain cars are backing up into the prairies. As a result of this situation millions of dollars are being lost each day this dispute and tie-up continue.
It is not my wish to detract at all from the case the hon. member has presented in respect of problems confronting St. Lawrence river ports, and I for one am prepared to support him in any effort to discuss and debate that situation. The government, I suggest, would be wise to agree to the suggestion that at some time early next week this whole question should be discussed. Nothing will be added so far as a solution to the problems facing Montreal, Quebec, and Trois-Rivieres are concerned by tying up ports in British Columbia. All that will result is an increase in human suffering and a tremendously enlarged economic loss to that part of Canada.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
Surely, if we are to have any type of national unity and national identity it will have to come from recognizing not only the problems in our own provinces and regions but understanding and appreciating the problems of people in other parts of Canada. I am sure the hon. member for Lapointe would feel very strongly if a strike, which was tying up the St. Lawrence ports and could be resolved by government action, was allowed to continue by reason of the lack of co-operation of some of us who come from the Pacific coast. I think he would resent that; I think his people would resent it. The hon. member must understand, equally that people in other parts of Canada will not feel kindly disposed to any hon. member preventing the government bringing in

legislation to solve this serious problem. I have not seen the legislation, but if it offers any hope at all that we can get the ports operating again I think the hon. member ought to give the government the opportunity to present the legislation and let the house discuss it and dispose of it one way or the other.
I do appeal to the hon. member, because I know he has a generous disposition, in the name of humanity and the welfare of the people on the Pacific coast not to take a step which can only increase bitterness and cause unnecessary hardship.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, numerous appeals have been made to my understanding, to my feelings of patriotism, to national unity, but no one among all those who made those appeals has suggested any action to solve other problems.
It has been pointed out that millions of dollars are lost, but nobody thinks of the millions of dollars being lost in the port of Montreal because of the tie-up of shipping.
Mention is made of British Columbia workers who experience hardships on account of that strike, but nothing is said about Montreal dockers who are out of work during the winter because that port is closed, as well as those in Trois-Rivieres and Quebec city.
Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to hear appeals, as long as mine are also heard. I do not turn them down, I am ready to accept them; but a deaf ear has been turned to my appeal. Nobody has agreed to discuss and solve the problem. This does not even require any legislation, only a decision by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill).
Not later than yesterday morning, the Minister of Transport warned that ships on the St. Lawrence could no longer rely on ice-breakers in winter-time.
Mr. Speaker, if you want me to hear the appeal, I am ready, but the others should also hear mine. I guess the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) is right; the wait and see policy of the government is probably responsible for the situation in which we find ourselves at the present time. I think he may be right about that. It is precisely because the government has stood still for many years with regard to winter navigation on the St. Lawrence, thus depriving-and I want to

make to everyone the same sentimental appeal which was made to me-the poor workers of Quebec city, Trois-Rivieres and Montreal of their means of livelihood in the dead of winter. But who is listening; what I am saying goes in one ear and out the other.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I say it and I repeat it: the appeal which was made to me, I am ready to listen to it, but on one condition, and I am laying down that condition, because I know that otherwise our appeals will never be heeded. We have been making that same appeal in Quebec for 20 years. But it has never been heard. If you want yours to be heard, you will also listen to our calls to reason.
Today, I am calling upon your good sense. And I say: I am ready to agree to that matter being discussed tomorrow morning, but I ask-and that is the condition-that we discuss also winter navigation on the St. Lawrence for the coming years, otherwise the harbours will stay closed. You want to open them? Well, open them all.
I am better than you are: you are appealing to me, to my sympathy to open the harbours in British Columbia. Very well. But open also the harbours in Montreal, Quebec city and Trois-Rivieres. Thus, they will all be open and everyone will be happy.
That is the national unity you should be talking about, not only in one place, but throughout the country. National unity is not a one-way street; it is not for a region only, but for all of them. If you want to open the harbours, open them up throughout Canada. That is what I want. Otherwise, Mr. Speaker, I will not agree.

The matter does not come under any legislation and should not be discussed here. All that is required is a decision by the Minister of Transport commissioning icebreakers working on the St. Lawrence to keep the channel open the year round. That is all there is to it.
And if the only promise I get is that the matter will be discussed further, well I do not go for that because we have had such promises for years with nothing ever materializing. I want to see action for once. Let us open those ports. Note that of all the suggestions made by hon. members to settle the whole matter, mine is the most logical because I go further in that I want to see as many ports as possible open to shipping and thus save as many million dollars as possible and provide jobs for as many people as possible.
